title: LEADERSHIP | 5.25.26 Team Members Who Wait to Be Told What to Do
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Common wisdom blames passive team members for waiting to be told what to do, attributing their behavior to low initiative or disengagement. The article argues, however, that the leader is usually the structural cause: when team members are only assigned tasks to execute, the pattern itself trains them to suspend initiative and wait for the next instruction. Leaders scratch their heads wondering why these team members seem less responsible, when the design they created is what produces that passivity. Breaking the cycle requires the leader to shift from taskmaster to coach—replacing task assignment with outcome ownership and leaving the how to the team member rather than prescribing every step. When people are genuinely entrusted with goals rather than steps, their engagement, resourcefulness, and drive emerge naturally. The piece emphasizes that ownership cannot be demanded; it must be invited through genuine trust. Leaders who make this structural shift reliably find the same individuals who once needed constant instruction begin anticipating problems and driving results without being asked.
points: * The leader, not the individual, is usually to blame when team members wait passively for instructions; the task-assignment pattern trains this behavior into the team. * Assigning tasks creates passive execution; assigning outcomes creates active ownership—initiative and resourcefulness emerge naturally when people control the how. * The difference between a team member who waits and one who acts is rarely a matter of character—it is a matter of how the work has been designed by the leader. * Ownership cannot be demanded; it must be invited through genuine trust that leaves the method in the hands of the team member. * Leaders who define outcomes rather than direct tasks will find the same people begin anticipating problems and proposing solutions without being prompted.
quotes: When team members are only assigned tasks to complete, they quickly become robots of execution. The pattern trains them to postpone any initiative and instead wait for the next instruction.
Good leaders try not to assign tasks. Instead, they ask team members to own projects and outcomes.

When team members are entrusted to decide how to achieve goals and not just execute critical steps in the process, they become active owners. Their engagement, initiative, and resourcefulness suddenly blossom.
The difference between a team member who waits and one who acts is rarely a matter of character. It is a matter of design.

Leaders who shift from directing work to defining outcomes will be surprised at how quickly the same people who once needed constant instruction begin anticipating problems, proposing solutions, and driving results without being asked.
Ownership cannot be demanded. It must be invited.
